title: Dividing a Whole Number by a Unit Fraction

steps.body: Dividing a whole number BY a unit fraction asks a different question: how many of that piece fit? Three wholes hold twelve fourths.
steps.narration: Dividing a whole number BY a unit fraction asks a different question: how many of that piece fit? Three wholes hold twelve fourths.

widget.prompt: How many fourths fit in 3 wholes? Build that count as ?/4.
widget.successFeedback: 12/4 — three wholes hold twelve fourths, which is why 3 ÷ 1/4 = 12.
widget.lowFeedback: That build is SHORTER than 12/4 — either shade more pieces or make each piece larger until the lengths match.
widget.highFeedback: That build is LONGER than 12/4 — either shade fewer pieces or make each piece smaller until the lengths match.

commonFractions.feedback: 3/4 is what 3 ÷ 4 gives — sharing three among four, not counting how many fourths fit.
4/4 is a single whole; three wholes hold three times as many fourths.

predict.reveal: Fourths are small, so a great many of them fit inside three wholes.

cml.actionGoal: Ask what is being cut and how big each piece is, then count the pieces for g5fd whole by unit.
invariants: Division and fractions are the same act seen twice: sharing a wholes among b people gives a/b, and dividing BY a piece asks how many of it fit, which is why g5fd whole by unit produces a larger answer when the divisor is under one.
misconceptions: Reading "divide by 1/4" as "take a quarter of", reporting a remainder when the leftover could be shared, or shrinking the pieces when only their count should change.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: If the divisor grew past one, would the answer become larger or smaller than the dividend?

widget.prompt: Compute 9 × 8 — the number of eighths that fit in 9 wholes.

commonErrors.feedback: Adding mixes a count of wholes with a piece size; each whole holds 8 eighths.
8 is how many eighths fit in ONE whole; there are 9 wholes here.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Ask what is being cut and what size the pieces are; the count of pieces is the answer.

widget.prompt: To model 3 ÷ 1/4, what does the picture show?

options.label: 12 fourths fit in 3 wholes
options.feedback: Correct — dividing by a fraction asks how many of that piece fit, and twelve fourths fit in three wholes.

options.label: 3 cut into 4 equal parts, giving 3/4
options.feedback: That models 3 ÷ 4. Dividing BY 1/4 asks how many fourths fit, which makes the answer larger.

options.label: 1/4 of 3, giving 3/4
options.feedback: That is 3 × 1/4. Dividing by a fraction below one makes the result bigger, not smaller.

options.label: Nothing — you cannot divide by a fraction
options.feedback: You can, and the question it answers is simply "how many of these fit?"

takeaways: Dividing by a fraction counts how many fit.
Small pieces mean a large count.
